## Base9 {#sec-b9 .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

Whereas [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} is like glue that allows us to combine [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} and [sid](#sid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval differences"}, Dec [nonary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_numeral_system#Compact_ternary_representation:_base_9_and_27:~:text=base%209%2C%20each%20digit%20is%20two%20ternary%20digits) ([base9]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="nonary"}) enables us to append [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}. The table below shows the [astronomical symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_symbol#:~:text=symbols%20used%20to%20represent%20astronomical%20objects) used by Dec for [base9]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="nonary"} ([b9](#b9){#base9 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}). When we replace the "decimilliday" ([dmd](#dmd){#decimilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"}) digit in a [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with a [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit, the [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit counts tens of [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} instead of [dmd](#dmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"} and the next digit tracks [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} instead of "centimillidays" ([cmd](#cmd){#centimilliday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}).

A [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with four [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, one [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, and one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit can match the time represented by any [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet, because the product of the bases of its digits is evenly divisible by the number of [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} in a day: 10000 &times; 9 &times; 24 &div; 86400 = 2160000 &div; 86400 = 25. For [hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"}, one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit is sufficient. The [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet selected by the range inputs below corresponds to [Hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"} \${b24hodHsl} and [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} \${hmsTodHsl}\${hmsSecHsl}\${hmsSidHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: hmsinput
//| class: slider
viewof hmsinput = Inputs.form([
  Inputs.range([0, 23], {label: "Hour", value: 11, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Minute", value: 0, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Second", value: 0, step: 1}),
])
```

In @tbl-time below, the [quotidie]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per day"} ([q](#q){#quotidie .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quotidie"}) column shows how many multiples of the unit in each row can fit into one day and the [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} column uses endings called Dec terminators to transform the fraction of a day that each unit represents from a repeating decimal into a [terminating decimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=a%20finite%20number%20of%20nonzero%20digits). The [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit in the terminators in @tbl-time represents 6 [decaseconds]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tens of seconds"} ([Ds](#decasec){#decasecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tens of seconds"}): 6 &div; 9 = 0.[♄]{.color6by9 .mono}.

## Base25 and base6 {#sec-b25 .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

Whereas [heh](#heh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Hipparchian equinoctial hours"}, "Birunian equinoctial minutes" ([bem](#bem){#birunianequinoctialminute .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Birunian equinoctial minutes"}), and "Birunian equinoctial seconds" ([bes](#bes){#birunianequinoctialsecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Birunian equinoctial seconds"}) divide a day into 24, 1440, and 86400 parts, Dec hours ([h](#h){#dechour .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec hours"}), Dec minutes ([m](#m){#decminute .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec minutes"}), and [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} divide a day into 25, 1500, and 90000 parts. One [h](#h){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec hour"} is 40 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}, 60 [m](#m){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec minutes"}, or 3600 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, one [m](#m){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec minute"} is 60 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, and one [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} is 90 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}. Dec writes the hour as one [pentavigesimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_numeral_systems#Standard_positional_numeral_systems) ([base25]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentavigesimal"}) digit, which is a letter of the [Ogham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogham) alphabet, as shown in @tbl-b25 below. Zero-based [base25]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="pentavigesimal"} ([b25](#b25){#base25 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base25"}) digits use the Ogham space mark ([&#x1680;]{.ogham}) for 0, whereas one-based [b25](#b25){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base25"} digits use ᚙ for 25 instead, like a 12-hour clock that shows 12 instead of 0.

Dec writes the minute and second as one [senary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senary) ([base6]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="senary"}) digit followed by one [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digit. The [base6]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="senary"} ([b6](#b6){#base6 .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base6"}) digits are [counting rods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_rods), and the number of horizontal strokes in each rod is its value, as shown in @tbl-b6 below.

Since the place value of each digit is the place value of the digit to its left divided by its own base, a Dec hour minute second is a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} written with one [b25](#b25){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base25"}, two [b6](#b6){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base6"}, and two [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, plus one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} [sid](#sid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="second interval difference"} digit when it does not land on a whole [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec second"}. The [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet selected by the range inputs above is \${decHmsHsl()} in Dec hours, minutes, and seconds.

# Coordinated Universal Time {#sec-utc .hiddenheading}

Rather than use a terminator as in @tbl-time, Dec expresses one [heh](#heh){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Hipparchian equinoctial hour"} in [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"} as a single [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit: 0.41[♄]{.color6by9 .mono} = [β]{.color1by24 .mono}. If we add [β]{.color1by24 .mono} [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"} to the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, we get the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} associated with the [UTC+1 offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%2B01:00#:~:text=a%20time%20offset%20from%20UTC%20of%20%2B01%3A00): 0.\${zeroTpadHsl()} + [β]{.color1by24 .mono} &div; 10 = 0.\${utc1tintHsl()}. Currently, the Zone [0]{.color0} Dec time is \${zeroTpadHsl()}&minus;[0]{.color0} and the UTC+1 Dec time is \${utc1tpadHsl()}&minus;[β]{.color1by24 .mono}. Dec times consist of a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, a minus sign (&minus;), and an offset.

There are 12 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that become terminating decimals after being converted from hours to days and therefore could be displayed in either [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} or [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Although it has only ten time zones, Dec can express any [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset using one or two non-negative [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. There are 27 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that require only one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit and 11 that need two [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits.

Out of the [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets) [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, 14 are negative (&lt;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) and 24 are non-negative (&ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}). The [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with [the most negative offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9212:00#:~:text=a%20nautical%20time%20zone%20comprising%20the%20high%20seas%20between%20180%C2%B0%20and%20172%C2%B030%E2%80%B2W%20longitude) is completely uninhabited. The bar chart below visualizes the population of each [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone based on 2020 [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) data. The vast majority of all people live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with &ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets.

{{< include /dec/time/_tzpopplot.qmd >}}

Negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets only exist in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas#:~:text=a%20landmass%20comprising%20the%20totality%20of%20North%20America%20and%20South%20America) and islands in the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Atlantic_Ocean) and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean) Oceans. Therefore, the bar chart above is essentially comparing the populations of the Americas and the rest of the world. According to 2021 [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs#:~:text=part%20of%20the%20United%20Nations%20Secretariat) data, roughly 1 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Americas.

Dec forbids the association of dates with negative offsets. Therefore, Dec will add ten [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to any negative offset and add one day to the date associated with that offset. Negative offset handling has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or the conversion of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and is typically only necessary after a "year month day" ([ymd](#ymd){#yearmonthday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"}) triplet is converted into a Dec date.

If we do not know whether Day [364]{.color364by365} belongs to a common or leap year, adding one day to it yields either Day [0]{.color0} or Day [365]{.color365by366} and this uncertainty is expressed as a [multiplication sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication_sign) over the last digit of [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0}. The sign hints that [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is short for [365]{.color0}&times;`leap`, where [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is either [365]{.color365by366} if `leap` is 1 or [0]{.color0} if `leap` is 0. We can find `leap` by passing any year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}) to @eq-leap below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07}
$$
\text{leap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} 100\neq0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-leap}

:::

# Day of week (dow) {#sec-dow .hiddenheading}

Adding one day to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, but it increments the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} and "day of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). Dec meets the expectations of [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20currently%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) users who live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with negative offsets by essentially deriving the previous [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} or [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} from the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} if a location in the Americas is provided without an offset or with a negative offset.

# Time zone offset (tzo) {#sec-tzo .hiddenheading}

In Dec, "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) are derived solely from longitude. Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"}), arcbeats ([a](#a){#arcbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}), or submultiples thereof. If we travel East or West until we reach our starting point, we will cover 1 [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} or 100000 ([10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}) [a](#a){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}. A [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} is essentially a [deciwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a wěi"} ([dw](#dw){#deciwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}) longitude that became a single-digit [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} integer via  [truncation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncation#Truncation_and_floor_function:~:text=truncation%20is%20limiting%20the%20number%20of%20digits%20right%20of%20the%20decimal%20point) or [flooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=takes%20as%20input%20a%20real%20number%20x%2C%20and%20gives%20as%20output%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x): &LeftFloor;\${longInputHsl} &div; 100&RightFloor; = \${longFloorHsl()}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput
//| class: slider
viewof lonInput = Inputs.range([0, 999], {label: "Longitude", value: 500, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: dstinput
//| class: interval
// https://observablehq.com/@mootari/range-slider
viewof dstspan = interval([0, 366], {
  step: 1,
  value: [7, 246],
  label: "Span",
})
```

The range input above selects a milliwěi ([mw](#mw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliwěi"}) longitude and the [interval](https://observablehq.com/@mootari/range-slider) input beneath it determines the start and end of "[daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time#:~:text=the%20practice%20of%20advancing%20clocks)" ([dst](#dst){#daylightsavingtime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"}) by selecting the "[dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"} initiation [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([did](#did){#dstinitdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time initiation day of year"}), which is the last [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} before [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"}, and the "[dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"} expiration [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}" ([ded](#ded){#dstexpdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time expiration day of year"}), which is the first [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} after [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"}. Dec represents [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"} by appending a minus sign, and [square brackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise) that contain an [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_%28mathematics%29#:~:text=a%20non%2Dequal%20comparison%20between%20two%20numbers%20or%20other%20mathematical%20expressions) to an a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}, : [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}&minus;\[[did](#did){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time initiation day of year"}<[doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}<[ded](#ded){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time expiration day of year"}\].

where [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} is the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} associated with the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} to which we are applying [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"}: \${longFloorHsl()}&minus;\${dstBracketHsl()}. 


When we combine with the current tod-tzo Dec time with the  is \${longTimeHsl()}&minus;\${longFloorHsl()} if the inequality is true or \${saveTimeHsl()}&minus;\${saveFloorHsl()} if the inequality is false, based on the selections above: \${currTimeHsl()}&minus;\${longFloorHsl()}&minus;\${dstBracketHsl()}. 

fall back doy (fbd)


[tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} selected above: , the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} adjusted by : [dst](#dst){#daylightsavingtime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"}, and the unadjusted [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} and the [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="daylight saving time"} expression: \${currTimeHsl()}&minus;\${longFloorHsl()}&minus;\${dstBracketHsl()}.

Together, the square brackets and the inequality represent either zero if the inequality is false or one if the inequality is true: 1 = [true]; 0 = [false].

with is based \${currTimeHsl()}&minus;\${currFloorHsl()} , on the selections above either with the adjusted [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}: \${currTimeHsl()}&minus;\${currFloorHsl()}, or with the unadjusted [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} and the [dst](#dst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}: 

[☿]{.color1by9 .mono} in [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, [1]{.color0} in [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, [β]{.color1by24 .mono} in [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} true bracket is [β]{.color1by24 .mono} and a false one is [α]{.color0 .mono}. In general, the Iverson bracket always matches the base of the offset that it adjusts. refers to intervals as spans and the terms minuend and subtrahend instead of start and end.

For example, if we want our [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} to change from [8]{.color008by365} gains 1 [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"} from Day [8]{.color008by365} to Day [245]{.color245by365} can be written as [8]{.color8}&minus;\[[7]{.color007by365}\${lt}\${zeroDotyHsl()}\${lt}[246]{.color246by365}\], which currently . Hour offsets work the same way: 500&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono}&minus;\[7<257<245\] is 500&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono} when the inequality is false and 541&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono}&minus;[β]{.color1by24 .mono} = 541&minus;[φ]{.color20by24 .mono} when it is true, which matches the shift from UTC&minus;5 to UTC&minus;4 in the eastern United States.

If we want the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} selected above to change from \${longFloorHsl()} to \${saveFloorHsl()} in between Day [7]{.color007by365} and Day [245]{.color245by365}, we can express it as \${longFloorHsl()}&minus;\[[7]{.color007by365}\${lt}\${zeroDotyHsl()}\${lt}[245]{.color245by365}\]. If the [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_%28mathematics%29#:~:text=a%20non%2Dequal%20comparison%20between%20two%20numbers%20or%20other%20mathematical%20expressions) is true, inside the [Iverson bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=1%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise) The current using this adjusted [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} is \${currTimeHsl()}&minus;\${currFloorHsl()}, because the [inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inequality_%28mathematics%29#:~:text=a%20non%2Dequal%20comparison%20between%20two%20numbers%20or%20other%20mathematical%20expressions) inside the [Iverson bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=1%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise) is \${longTest}. Instead of a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}, we can use a different offset 500&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono}&minus;\[7<257<245\] is 500&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono} when the inequality is false and 541&minus;[υ]{.color19by24 .mono}&minus;[β]{.color1by24 .mono} = 541&minus;[φ]{.color20by24 .mono} when it is true, which matches the shift from UTC&minus;5 to UTC&minus;4 in the eastern United States.

# Daylight saving time {#sec-dst .hiddenheading}

Although Dec time zones never change their respective [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}, Dec can express [daylight saving time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daylight_saving_time#:~:text=the%20practice%20of%20advancing%20clocks) using the [Iverson bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iverson_bracket#:~:text=is%20defined%20to%20take%20the%20value%201%20for%20the%20values%20of%20the%20variables%20for%20which%20the%20statement%20is%20true%2C%20and%20takes%20the%20value%200%20otherwise). In [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, an Iverson bracket evaluates to one if the inequality inside it is true and zero otherwise. In [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}, a true bracket is [β]{.color1by24 .mono} and a false one is [α]{.color0 .mono}. In general, the Iverson bracket always matches the base of the offset that it adjusts.


The [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is approximately ([~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}) 1 [taur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="circumference = 𝜏r"} ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"} [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) long. Near the Equator, a longitude that has a [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_degrees#Precision) of 0.1 [microwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of wěi"} ([&micro;w](#uw){#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microwěi"}) or 10 milliarcbeats ([ma](#ma){#milliarcbeats .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}) is accurate to within [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.1 [microtaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of taur"} ([&micro;c](#uc){#microtaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microtaur"}), [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}10 "zone equatorial meters" ([zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), or 4 [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre#Definition:~:text=the%20base%20unit%20of%20length%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units), which is about the width of a [U-shaped living room layout](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/living-room-layouts) or the length of a typical [subcompact car](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/subcompact-cars-b-segment).

For precise [geopositioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopositioning#:~:text=estimating%20the%20geographic%20position%20of%20an%20object%20or%20a%20person), we may want to express [geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) in [ma](#ma){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}, but we are unlikely to need [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} when displaying the [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) or estimates of what the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will be when the Sun rises, reaches its [highest point of the day](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon), or sets. By default, Dec uses [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} precision to display a solar time and the "solar time offset" ([sto](#sto){#solartimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}) used to produce it.

# Solar time offset (sto) {#sec-sto .hiddenheading}

In Dec, any offset can be called a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} or a [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"}, because there will always be a longitude at which the sum of the given offset and the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will yield solar time or [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"}. In contrast, Dec has only ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, one for each of its ten time zones. Dec translates [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to Zone [0]{.color0} and UTC&minus;12 or UTC+12 to Zone [5]{.color5}, but does not categorize any other UTC offset as a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}.

Dec permits any non-negative offset that is less than one day and can be written with a finite number of [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. When a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or an offset does not have a decimal separator, its measurement unit is a submultiple of a day equal to 10^-[til](#til){#timeintegerlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"}^ days, where [til](#til){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"} is its "time integer length", its [level of precision](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_(numbers)#:~:text=level%20of%20exactness%20in%20a%20number%27s%20digits), or its digit count including any [leading zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leading_zero#:~:text=any%200%20digit%20that%20comes%20before%20the%20first%20nonzero%20digit).

[Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm#:~:text=the%20capital%20and%20most%20populous%20city%20of%20Sweden), the capital city of [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden#:~:text=a%20Nordic%20country%20located%20on%20the%20Scandinavian%20Peninsula%20in%20Northern%20Europe)🇸🇪, is located at [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[1]{.color1} [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}, almost exactly on the border between Zones [0]{.color0} and [1]{.color1}. A longitude of [1]{.color1} [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} corresponds to a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of [05]{.color05}. The [til](#til){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"} of [05]{.color05} is 2 and therefore its measurement unit is the centiday ([cd](#cd){#centiday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}), which is 10^-2^ days. We can use a multiplicative [conversion factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_of_units#:~:text=changes%20the%20unit%20without%20changing%20the%20quantity) of 10^-2^ to convert [cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"} to [d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}: 5 &times; 10^-2^ = 0.[05]{.color05}.

Dec uses [currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency#:~:text=a%20standardized%20form%20of%20money%20used%20as%20a%20medium%20of%20exchange) names for [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}: [dimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dime#Coins:~:text=coin%29%2C%20a-,ten%2Dcent%20coin,-and%20subunit%20of), [cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}: [cents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent#Currency:~:text=a%20one%2Dhundredth%20subdivision%20of%20several%20units%20of%20currency) (&cent;), and [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"}: [mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_(currency)#:~:text=a%20subunit%20of%20currency%2C%20used%20in%20several%20countries%20as%201%E2%81%841000%20of%20the%20base%20unit) (₥). Drawing inspiration from music and writing, Dec refers to [dmd](#dmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"} as "lines" ([l](#l){#line .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lines"}) and [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} as "beats" ([b](#b){#beat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"}). In [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry#:~:text=a%20form%20of%20literary%20art%20that%20uses%20aesthetic%20and%20often%20rhythmic%5B1%5D%5B2%5D%5B3%5D%20qualities%20of%20language%20to%20evoke%20meanings) and [playwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playwright#:~:text=For%20the%20ancient%20Greeks%2C%20playwriting%20involved%20po%C3%AFesis%2C%20%22the%20act%20of%20making%22.%20This%20is%20the%20source%20of%20the%20English%20word%20poet.), notably the [works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_William_Shakespeare#:~:text=39%20plays%20and%20154%20sonnets) of [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare#:~:text=an%20English%20playwright%2C%20poet%20and%20actor), [decasyllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decasyllable#:~:text=a%20poetic%20meter%20of%20ten%20syllables) and [iambic pentameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iambic_pentameter#:~:text=the%20rhythm%2C%20or%20meter%2C%20established%20by%20the%20words%20in%20each%20line) mandate ten [syllables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable#:~:text=a%20basic%20unit%20of%20organization%20within%20a%20sequence%20of%20speech%20sounds) per [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_%28poetry%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20writing%20into%20which%20a%20poem%20or%20play%20is%20divided%3A%20literally%2C%20a%20single%20row%20of%20text). In music, [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line#Terminology_2:~:text=a%20strand%20or%20melody%20of%20music%20played%20by%20an%20individual%20instrument%20or%20voice), [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody#:~:text=a%20linear%20succession%20of%20musical%20tones%20that%20the%20listener%20perceives%20as%20a%20single%20entity), [part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part_%28music%29#:~:text=a%20component%20of%20a%20musical%20composition), and [tune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music#Tune:~:text=a%20short%20instrumental%20piece) are synonyms. 

::: {.callout-warning}
# Bad Pun Alert
It took me forever and a **deciday** to come up with a pun for Declock⏰. I kept **second**-guessing myself and got really **wound** up, so I decided to take a **beat**. Then, I **zoned** out until it finally **struck** me: it's about **time**!
:::

# Mean solar time {#sec-mst .hiddenheading}

Outside of Dec, longitudes are often provided in [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_meridian_&28Greenwich&29#:~:text=a%20geographical%20reference%20line%20that%20passes%20through%20the%20Royal%20Observatory%2C%20Greenwich%2C%20in%20London%2C%20England) [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20measurement%20of%20a%20plane%20angle%20in%20which%20one%20full%20rotation%20is%20assigned%20the%20value%20of%20360%20degrees) ([g°](#gdeg){#greenwichdegrees .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"}). @eq-deg2wei converts [g°](#gdeg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"} to [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} and @eq-wei2deg does the opposite. To obtain a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}, we can pass [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} to @eq-wei2sto or [g°](#gdeg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"} to @eq-deg2sto below. As shown in @eq-mst below, we can sum an [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} with the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} to get a yearly average of solar time called "[mean solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Mean_solar_time:~:text=it%20follows%20an%20imaginary%20%22mean%20Sun%22%20that%20moves%20along%20the%20celestial%20equator%20at%20a%20constant%20rate%20that%20matches%20the%20real%20Sun%27s%20average%20rate%20over%20the%20year)" ([mst](#mst){#meansolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09}
$$\text{w} = (\text{g}^\circ + 378) \div 360 \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-deg2wei}

$$\text{g}^\circ = (\text{w} + 0.45) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 360 - 180$$ {#eq-wei2deg}

$$\text{sto} = (0.95 + \text{w}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-wei2sto}

$$\text{sto} = (\text{g}^\circ + 360) \div 360 \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-deg2sto}

$$\text{mst} = (\text{tod} + \text{sto}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-mst}
:::

# Equation of time (eot) {#sec-eot .hiddenheading}

If we want to tailor our solar time calculations to a specific [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} instead of an average for the entire year, we can calculate "[apparent solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Apparent_solar_time:~:text=the%20apparent%20motion%20of%20the%20actual%20Sun)" ([ast](#ast){#apparentsolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}) by summing [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} with the "[equation of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_time#:~:text=the%20discrepancy%20between%20two%20kinds%20of%20solar%20time)" ([eot](#eot){#equationoftime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}), as shown in @eq-ast.
Obtaining the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} requires a "time of year" ([toy](#toy){#timeofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}), which is an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} that was converted from days to years as displayed in @eq-toy.

To obtain a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}, we divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} by a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which is the number of days in the year. Dec passes the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} directly from @eq-toy to the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} function in @eq-eot without first multiplying it by 2𝜋 or 𝜏 to convert it from [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}) to [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}) because the [sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20side%20opposite%20that%20angle%20to%20the%20length%20of%20the%20longest%20side%20of%20the%20triangle) and [cos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20adjacent%20leg%20to%20that%20of%20the%20hypotenuse) [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions#:~:text=functions%20which%20relate%20an%20angle%20of%20a%20right%2Dangled%20triangle%20to%20ratios%20of%20two%20side%20lengths) used by Dec are designed for [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10}
$$\text{ast} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w} +  \text{eot}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-ast}

$$\text{toy} = \text{ada} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toy}

$$\text{syl} = \text{leap} + 365$$ {#eq-syl}

$$\begin{split}
\text{eot} & = \beta_0 \\
& + \beta_1 \times \text{cos(toy)} \\
& + \beta_2 \times \text{sin(toy)} \\
& + \beta_3 \times \text{cos(2} \times \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_4 \times \text{sin(2} \times \text{toy)}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-eot}
:::

By comparing the `sincost` and `sincos` functions, the code below demonstrates that using [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} rather than [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} can [yield more accurate results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=Representing%20angles%20in%20turns%20or%20half%2Dturns%20has%20accuracy%20advantages). Whereas `sincost` expects to receive [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} and is always correct, `sincos` assumes that it will get [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} and generates the slightly incorrect [E notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_notation#E_notation) values below because it cannot produce zero unless its input is zero.

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
sincost(x) = sincospi(2 * x)
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
sincospi = require(
  'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/stdlib-js/math-base-special-sincospi@umd/browser.js'
  )
function sincost(x) {
  return sincospi(2 * x);
}
function sincos(x) {
  return [Math.sin(x), Math.cos(x)]
}
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(1 * 2 * Math.PI)
```

### Python

```{python}
from math import cos, sin, pi, cospi, sinpi

def sincost(x):
    x *= 2
    return sinpi(x), cospi(x)

def sincos(x):
    return sin(x), cos(x)

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### R

```{r}
sincost <- function(x) {
  x <- 2 * x
  c(sinpi(x), cospi(x))
}

sincos <- function(x) {
  c(sin(x), cos(x))
}

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

:::

The values below are the coefficients of a [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic#:~:text=positive%20integer%20multiple%20of%20the%20fundamental%20frequency) [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model#:~:text=embodies%20a%20set%20of%20statistical%20assumptions%20concerning%20the%20generation%20of%20sample%20data), adapted from the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.noaa.gov) ([NOAA](#noaa){#nationaloceanicandatmosphericadministration .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"}) [General Solar Position Calculations](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/solareqns.PDF). Before [fitting](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.curve_fit.html) the model to [NOAA](#noaa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"} [yearly solar data](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/calcdetails.html), Dec divides [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values by 1.44 to convert [bem](#bem){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Birunian equinoctial minutes"} to [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}, converts [ymd](#ymd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"} triplet dates and [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet times into [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"}, and sorts by [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

{{< embed eot.ipynb#eotcoef >}}

{{< include /dec/time/_eotplot.qmd >}}

In the [line📈chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_chart#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20chart%20that%20displays%20information%20as%20a%20series%20of%20data%20points%20called%20%27markers%27%20connected%20by%20straight%20line%20segments) above, the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values range from -9.8 to 11.4 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} and the range of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [-365]{.color0} to [365]{.color365by366}, represents a common year followed by a leap year. The [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} reaches about one [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredth of a day"} ([cd]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}) on Days [245]{.color245by365} and [349]{.color349by365}, but passes through zero on Days [45]{.color045by365}, [103]{.color103by365}, [184]{.color184by365}, and [299]{.color299by365}. Therefore, [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} are equivalent four times per year.

Apart from transforming an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} into an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, we can also use [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values to more accurately estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow), sunrise, and sunset. @eq-solarnoon below creates a [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow) [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by keeping only the decimal part of the result of subtracting a [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} longitude and an [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} value that is measured in days from the sum of 9.55 and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} that is measured in days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11}
$$\text{solarnoon} = \left(9.55 + \text{tzo} - \text{w} - \text{eot}\right) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-solarnoon}
:::

# Cambridge and Cambridge {#sec-cac .hiddenheading}

To compare the solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in two cities, we can plug the longitude of each city into @eq-solarnoon above. If all of the variables other than longitude in @eq-solarnoon are set to zero, the resulting solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is almost five [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge#:~:text=a%20city%20and%20non%2Dmetropolitan%20district%20in%20the%20county%20of%20Cambridgeshire%2C%20England) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom#:~:text=a%20country%20in%20Northwestern%20Europe) and nearly seven [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts#:~:text=a%20city%20in%20Middlesex%20County%2C%20Massachusetts%2C%20United%20States) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States#:~:text=a%20country%20primarily%20located%20in%20North%20America).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12}
$$4.99635 = (9.55 - 0.050365) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk}

$$6.97516 = (9.55 - 0.852484) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema}
:::

The two homonymous cities are about two [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} apart and therefore will always differ by around two [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} in solar time, regardless of what time zone we use as our frame of reference. England is in Zone [0]{.color0} and Massachusetts is in Zone [8]{.color8}. From the perspective of Zone [8]{.color8}, solar noon is roughly [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [5]{.color5} in Cambridge, MA and about [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [3]{.color3} in Cambridge, UK.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13}
$$2.99635 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.050365) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk8}

$$4.97516 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.852484) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema8}
:::

# Light arc whole (law) {#sec-law .hiddenheading}

The path in the sky that the Sun appears to follow from a sunrise to a sunset is a "light [arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_path#:~:text=arc%2Dlike%20path%20that%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20follow%20across%20the%20sky) whole" ([law](#law){#lightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}). Solar noon, the midpoint of a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}, is halfway between sunrise and sunset. A [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} can be evenly split into two "light arc halves" ([lah](#lah){#lightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"}). Whereas [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} are time points, [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc wholes"} and [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc halves"} are durations. The difference between a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} is a sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.

## Night arc whole (naw) {#sec-naw .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

The Sun continues its path after it disappears below the horizon, moving from sunset to sunrise along a "night arc whole" ([naw](#naw){#nightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"}). Like [conjugate angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=conjugate%20angles%20sum%20to%20a%20full%20angle), a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} form a full circle that represents one day. Likewise, a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} and a "night arc half" ([nah](#nah){#nightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc half"}) are like two [supplementary angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=sum%20to%20a%20straight%20angle) that form a semicircle from solar noon to the [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} midpoint: [solar midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight#:~:text=the%20time%20opposite%20to%20solar%20noon%2C%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20closest%20to%20the%20nadir%2C%20and%20the%20night%20is%20equidistant%20from%20dusk%20and%20dawn).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14}
$$\text{law} = \text{lah} \times 2$$ {#eq-law}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunrise}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} \\
& = \text{sunset} - \text{law}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunrise}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunset}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{sunrise} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} + \text{lah} \\
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunset}

$$\text{naw} = \text{nah} \times 2$$ {#eq-naw}

$$\begin{split}
\text{day}
& = \text{law} + \text{naw} \\
& = (\text{lah} + \text{nah}) \times 2
\end{split}$$ {#eq-day}

$$\text{nah} = 0.5 - \text{lah}$$ {#eq-nah}

$$\begin{split}
\text{solarmidnight}
&= \text{sunrise} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{sunset} - \text{law} - \text{nah}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-solarmidnight}
:::

The range input below controls the yellow [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and the blue [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} in the diagram beneath it. At the Equator, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is always roughly half a day. During an equinox, the Sun rises a quarter turn from North and sets three quarter turns from North, so its sunrise and sunset azimuths happen to differ by the same half: 75% &minus; 25% = 50%. On other days, sunrise and sunset shift toward North or South, but the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} at the Equator stays about half a day. If the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is zero, a [polar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_night#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20below%20the%20horizon%20for%20more%20than%2024%C2%A0hours) occurs. A day without a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} is called a [polar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20visible%20at%20the%20local%20midnight).

{{< include /dec/time/_dayarcplot.qmd >}}

# Solar azimuth angle (saa) {#sec-saa .hiddenheading}

The numbers in the diagram above are "[solar azimuth angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_azimuth_angle#:~:text=horizontal%20angle%20with%20respect%20to%20north)" ([saa](#saa){#solarazimuthangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} ([mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}). At solar noon, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is 0 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} if the latitude is less than the "solar [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination#:~:text=the%20angular%20distance%20from%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere) angle" ([sda](#sda){#solardeclinationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}), as it always is outside the [tropics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropics#:~:text=the%20regions%20of%20Earth%20surrounding%20the%20equator) in the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20%28hemisphere%29%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20south%20of%20the%20equator) and 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} if the latitude is greater than the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}, as it always is outside the tropics in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator). The [radio](https://observablehq.github.io/framework/inputs/radio#:~:text=allows%20the%20user%20to%20choose%20one%20of%20a%20given%20set%20of%20values)📻input above controls whether the midpoint of the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is 0 or 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}. To measure the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} during the [daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location), point a compass🧭at the spot on the horizon below the Sun.

# Solar elevation angle (sea) {#sec-sea .hiddenheading}

During an [equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator) at the Equator, the Sun goes from East to West directly overhead, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} flips like a switch from 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} to 0.75 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} at solar noon, the "[solar elevation angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_zenith_angle#Summary_of_special_angles:~:text=For%20example%2C%20the-,solar,-elevation%20angle%20is)" ([sea](#sea){#solarelevationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}) peaks at 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}, and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} is 0.5 &minus; sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) &times; (0.25 &minus; [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}). To obtain the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, we can use the height (h) of a vertical rod on a level surface and the length (L) of its shadow: [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} = atan2(h, L).

# Inverse trigonometric functions {#sec-itf .hiddenheading}

In addition to determining the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, the  [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) function can also be used to calculate [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, as shown in @eq-astjing, where [j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is a latitude measured in turns called [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}). In Dec, [inverse trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions#:~:text=obtain%20an%20angle%20from%20any%20of%20the%20angle%27s%20trigonometric%20ratios) functions like [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) yield [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} as opposed to [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. At the Equator ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0), the latitude is zero and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 + atan2(-sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"})cos([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}), sin([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"})).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{atan2}\!\!\left(
\begin{aligned}
& \text{-sin(saa)cos(sea),} \\
& \text{sin(sea)cos(j) } - \\
& \text{cos(saa)cos(sea)sin(j)}
\end{aligned}
\right)
$$ {#eq-astjing}

$$
\text{ast} =
\begin{cases}
\text{saa} & \text{j} = 0.25 \\
0.5 + \text{atan2(-sin(saa)cos(sea), sin(sea))} & \text{j} = 0 \\
(1.5 - \text{saa}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 & \text{j} = -0.25
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-extremes}
:::

At the North Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0.25), the latitude is 0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. At the South Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = -0.25), the latitude is -0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 &minus; [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} before solar noon or [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 1.5 &minus; [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} after solar noon. In between the Equator and the South or North Pole (-0.25 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0 &or; 0 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0.25), we should use Equation -@eq-ast, -@eq-astjing, or -@eq-astsha.

Unlike @eq-astjing, @eq-astsha requires a [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. Whereas latitude is the angle from the Equator in the [geographic coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20spherical%20or%20geodetic%20coordinate%20system%20for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude), declination is the angle from the [celestial equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_equator) in the [equatorial coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20celestial%20coordinate%20system%20widely%20used%20to%20specify%20the%20positions%20of%20celestial%20objects). For simplicity, we can use the harmonic model in @eq-eot, with a separate set of fitted coefficients, for both the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. The line plot below shows [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angles"} over the course of a year.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{arccos}\!\!\left(\dfrac{\text{sin(sea)} - \text{sin(j)sin(sda)}}{\text{cos(j)cos(sda)}}\right) \times
\begin{cases}
\text{-}1 & 0 \le \text{saa} < 0.5 \\
1 & 0.5 \le \text{saa} < 1
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-astsha}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sda} & = \gamma_0 \\
& + \gamma_1 \times \text{cos(toy)} \\
& + \gamma_2 \times \text{sin(toy)} \\
& + \gamma_3 \times \text{cos(2} \times \text{toy)} \\
& + \gamma_4 \times \text{sin(2} \times \text{toy)}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sda}
:::

{{< include /dec/time/_sdaplot.qmd >}}

In the line plot above, [zero crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_crossing#:~:text=a%20point%20where%20the%20sign%20of%20a%20mathematical%20function%20changes) are [equinoxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator%2C%20rather%20than%20to%20its%20north%20or%20south) and [stationary points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_point#:~:text=a%20point%20on%20the%20graph%20of%20the%20function%20where%20the%20function%27s%20derivative%20is%20zero) are [solstices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solstice#:~:text=the%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20reaches%20its%20most%20northerly%20or%20southerly%20sun%20path%20relative%20to%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere). From the northward to the southward equinox, the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is positive and every [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} in the Northern Hemisphere is longer than the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} at the Equator, which is longer than every [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} in the Southern Hemisphere. The opposite is true from the southward to the northward equinox.

The chart below splits the [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) population data into two bars representing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and then further divides each bar by [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset. Nearly 7 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Northern Hemisphere and therefore experience the longest [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of the year at the [northern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_solstice#:~:text=In%20the%20Northern%20Hemisphere%2C%20the%20June%20solstice%20is%20the%20summer%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20longest%20period%20of%20daylight%29%2C%20while%20in%20the%20Southern%20Hemisphere%20it%20is%20the%20winter%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20shortest%20period%20of%20daylight%29).

{{< include /dec/time/_hemipopplot.qmd >}}

The top range input below picks the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that we will turn into a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} and then pass to our [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model. The two range inputs beneath the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input choose the geographic coordinates needed to find the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}. While the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} rely on all three range inputs, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} depends on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and latitude but not on longitude: \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} &minus; \${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17}
$$\text{sunset} - \text{sunrise} = \text{law}$$ {#eq-lawdiff}

$$\text{lah} = \text{arccos}(\max(\text{-}1, \min(1, \text{x})))$$ {#eq-lah}

$$\text{x} = \dfrac{\text{sin(-0.002314)} - \text{sin(j)sin(sda)}}{\text{cos(j)cos(sda)}}$$ {#eq-lahx}
:::

@eq-lah computes the [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} from the latitude ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}) and the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. At sunrise and sunset, the center of the Sun is about 0.002314 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} (0.833 degrees) below the horizon, because the atmosphere bends sunlight and the top edge of the Sun appears before its center, so @eq-lah puts a [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} of -0.002314 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} into the arccos part of @eq-astsha. Limiting the fraction to the range from -1 to 1 makes the [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} 0 during a polar night and 0.5 during a polar day.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: doyinput
//| class: slider
viewof doyInput = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day of year", value: 183, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: latinput
//| class: slider
viewof latInput = Inputs.range([-250, 250], {label: "Latitude", value: 0, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput1
//| class: slider
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 1000], {label: "Longitude", value: 500, step: 1}), viewof lonInput)
```

In the equation above, the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is the [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted), the sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is the [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted), and the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is the [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference): sunset &minus; sunrise = [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}. If we replace the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, the difference will no longer be the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} but rather the time until sunset if it is negative or since sunset if it is positive: \${selectedCurrent.toFixed(3)} = \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} [${selectedDifference < 0 ? "-" : "+"}]{.mono} \${parseFloat(Math.abs(selectedDifference).toFixed(3))}.

# Current elapsed remaining {#sec-cer .hiddenheading}

In general, the subtrahend is the time of an event such as a rocket🚀launch and the difference is the negative [remaining time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event) if the minuend is less than the subtrahend or the positive [elapsed time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Elapsed_Time) if the minuend is greater than the subtrahend. When the minuend is the current time, the difference acts as a "[T minus (T&minus;) countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining)" or "[T plus (T+) countup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=After%20a%20launch%2C%20most%20countdown%20clocks%20begin%20to%20show%20Mission%20Elapsed%20Time)".

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18}
$$\begin{cases}\text{difference}<0&{\text{if } \text{minuend} < \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}=0&{\text{if minuend} = \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}>0&{\text{if minuend}>\text{subtrahend.}}\end{cases}$$ {#eq-difference}
:::

# Webpage load time {#sec-wlt .hiddenheading}

The difference between a minuend and subtrahend is intended to be a duration, whereas the minuend and subtrahend themselves are supposed to be [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} that represent [time points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_point#:~:text=an%20instant%2C%20analogous%20to%20a%20geometrical%20point%20in%20space). If the minuend is the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the subtrahend is the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} when this webpage loaded, the difference will be the duration since this webpage loaded: \${zeroTintHsl()} = \${loadTimeHsl()} + \${elaTimeHsl()}. 

# Positive interval tod (pit) {#sec-pit .hiddenheading}

A [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can be either a "positive interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([pit](#pit){#positiveintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"}) that counts up the time since the "beginning of day" ([bod](#bod){#beginningofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of day"}) or a "negative interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([nit](#nit){#negativeintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}) that counts down the time until the "end of day" ([eod](#eod){#endofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"}). The difference between a [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} and an [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} is a [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}: [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} &minus; [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} = [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}. The [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} is equal to one day or [10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"} [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}. In [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}, the current Zone [0]{.color0} [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} is \${zeroTintHsl()} &minus; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0} = \${negaTintHsl()}. 

# Positive integer doy (pid) {#sec-pid .hiddenheading}

Similarly, a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} can be either a "positive integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([pid](#pid){#positiveintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}) that counts up the days since the "beginning of year" ([boy](#boy){#beginningofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}) or a "negative integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([nid](#nid){#negativeintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) that counts down the days until the "end of year" ([eoy](#eoy){#endofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}) and an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} can be either a "positive interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([pia](#pia){#positiveintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"}) that joins a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} and [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} or a "negative interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([nia](#nia){#negativeintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"}) that links a [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} and [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}: [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"} = [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} + [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} = [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} &minus; [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}.

When a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} are in the same equation, we multiply the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by a conversion factor or divide it by an inverse conversion factor so that its measurement unit matches that of the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}: \${zeroDotyHsl()}.\${zeroTpadHsl()} = \${zeroDotyHsl()} + \${zeroTintHsl()} &div; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0} = \${nextDotyHsl()} + \${negaTintHsl()} &div; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0}. If the subtrahend is an [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"}, it disappears after advancing the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} by one day and turning the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} into a [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}.

# Year of era (yoe) {#sec-yoe .hiddenheading}

Likewise, a subtrahend that is an [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} is not displayed as part of a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} or an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} because it becomes incorporated into the "year of era" ([yoe](#yoe){#yearofera .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}): \${zeroYearHsl()} + \${zeroDotyHsl()}.\${zeroTpadHsl()} &div; [\${zeroNdaysInYear}]{.color0} = \${nextYearHsl()} + \${zeroNidHsl()}.\${negaTendHsl()} &div; [\${zeroNdaysInYear}]{.color0}. Essentially, the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} takes up any amount of time that spills over from the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} absorbs any amount of time that does not fit into the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}.
